entries.topicDescription: Powerful operations on lists, sets, and maps.

tips.title: windowed() and chunked() give you sliding vs non-overlapping batches
tips.content:
windowed(size, step) produces overlapping sliding windows over a
collection — useful for moving averages or comparing consecutive pairs.
chunked(size) instead splits the collection into non-overlapping batches
of the given size, useful for pagination-style processing.

Both accept an optional transform lambda applied to each window/chunk
directly, avoiding a separate map() call afterward.
tips.codeSnippet:
val prices = listOf(10, 12, 9, 15, 20)
val movingAverages = prices.windowed(3) { it.average() } // overlapping windows of 3
val batches = prices.chunked(2) // [[10,12],[9,15],[20]] — non-overlapping

tips.title: zip() pairs two collections element-by-element for combined processing
tips.content:
Manually indexing into two parallel lists (names[i] with ages[i]) is
error-prone if the lists ever get out of sync in length, and reads less
clearly than expressing the intent directly.

zip() combines two collections into a list of Pairs (or a custom-typed
result via a transform lambda), truncating to the shorter collection's
length automatically rather than throwing on a length mismatch.

tips.title: flatMap avoids nested collections that map alone would produce
tips.content:
Calling map { it.subItems } on a list of parents produces a
List<List<SubItem>> — a nested structure that then requires a separate
flatten() call, or manual double-iteration, to work with as a single flat
list.

flatMap does both steps in one pass: it maps each element to a collection
and flattens the results into a single list directly, which is both more
efficient (single traversal) and clearer at the call site.

tips.title: scan() emits every intermediate accumulator value, unlike fold
tips.content:
fold() only returns the final accumulated result, discarding every
intermediate value along the way — but sometimes you need the running
total at each step, not just the end result (a running balance, a
progress percentage over time).

scan() works like fold but returns a list of every intermediate
accumulator state, including the initial value as the first element,
giving you the full accumulation history in one call.

tips.title: Chain compareBy/thenBy to build multi-field comparators declaratively
tips.content:
Writing a manual Comparator with nested if/else branches to sort by one
field and break ties with another is verbose and easy to get the tie-
breaking order wrong in.

compareBy { } builds a Comparator from a selector, and thenBy { } chains
an additional tie-breaking selector — compareByDescending and
thenByDescending cover the reverse-order cases, all composable in one
readable expression.

tips.title: buildList/buildMap/buildSet enable imperative construction with an immutable result
tips.content:
Building a collection with conditional logic (looping, branching on
conditions to decide what to add) often means creating a mutable
collection, populating it imperatively, then exposing it as read-only
afterward — two separate steps with a manual conversion between them.

buildList {} (and its map/set equivalents) gives you a MutableList
receiver inside the lambda for imperative construction, but returns an
immutable List from the call itself — combining imperative-friendly
construction with an immutable public result in one expression.

tips.title: Primitive arrays (IntArray, LongArray) avoid boxing overhead
tips.content:
A List<Int> stores boxed Integer objects on the JVM — each element is a
separate heap-allocated object, adding both memory overhead and
indirection cost compared to a raw primitive array.

IntArray, LongArray, DoubleArray, and similar specialized types store
unboxed primitives contiguously in memory, which matters for
performance-sensitive code processing large numeric datasets — Kotlin's
standard library provides IntArray-specific versions of common operations
like map, filter, and sum.
tips.codeSnippet:
val boxed: List<Int> = List(1_000_000) { it } // 1M boxed Integer objects
val unboxed: IntArray = IntArray(1_000_000) { it } // contiguous primitives, no boxing

tips.title: generateSequence produces lazy, potentially infinite sequences
tips.content:
Building a sequence of values determined by a recurrence relation (each
value derived from the previous one) doesn't fit neatly into eager
collection-building, especially when the sequence has no natural upper
bound known in advance.

generateSequence(seed) { next } lazily produces values one at a time based
on a next-value function, stopping only when that function returns null —
combined with takeWhile or take(), this safely handles infinite or
unbounded sequences without ever materializing the whole thing.

tips.title: groupBy with a valueTransform reshapes grouped data in one pass
tips.content:
groupBy { keySelector } alone groups full elements under each key — but
often you only need a derived value per group (just the names, not the
full objects), which would otherwise require a second map() pass over
each group afterward.

groupBy(keySelector, valueTransform) applies the transform during the
same single pass that builds the groups, avoiding the extra iteration over
every group's contents.

tips.title: binarySearch requires a pre-sorted collection or it silently misbehaves
tips.content:
Collection.binarySearch() runs in O(log n) but relies on the collection
already being sorted according to the same comparator (or natural order)
you search with — calling it on unsorted data doesn't throw, it just
returns an incorrect, meaningless result.

Only reach for binarySearch on data you've explicitly sorted (or received
pre-sorted, like from a paginated, ordered API) — for unsorted data,
indexOfFirst is the correct O(n) alternative, not a silently-wrong O(log n)
one.
tips.codeSnippet:
val sorted = listOf(1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11)
val index = sorted.binarySearch(7) // 3 — correct, because the list is sorted

val unsorted = listOf(5, 1, 9, 3)
unsorted.binarySearch(3) // undefined/incorrect result — never sorted first

tips.title: listOf() vs mutableListOf() — choose based on whether you need to modify it
tips.content:
listOf() returns a read-only List with no add/remove methods available at
all, while mutableListOf() returns a MutableList that supports adding,
removing, and updating elements.

Default to listOf() unless you specifically need to mutate the collection
after creation — exposing read-only types by default communicates intent
and prevents accidental mutation from code that shouldn't be changing the
data.
tips.codeSnippet:
val fixedItems = listOf("a", "b", "c") // fixedItems.add(...) won't compile
val editableItems = mutableListOf("a", "b", "c")
editableItems.add("d") // works

tips.title: Use firstOrNull()/lastOrNull() to avoid crashing on empty collections
tips.content:
first() and last() throw a NoSuchElementException if the collection is
empty, which is easy to overlook when working with data that might
legitimately be empty (search results, filtered lists).

firstOrNull()/lastOrNull() return null instead of throwing, letting you
handle the empty case explicitly with the Elvis operator or a null check,
rather than needing a try/catch around a simple lookup.

tips.title: forEach is for simple iteration without needing an index or early exit
tips.content:
forEach reads more concisely than a for-loop when you just need to perform
an action per element and don't need the index or the ability to break
early — note that a `return` inside a forEach lambda returns from the
lambda's enclosing function, not just that iteration, which can surprise
newcomers.

For cases needing the index, use forEachIndexed; for cases needing to
break or continue mid-iteration, a regular for-loop is more appropriate
since forEach can't be interrupted early with break/continue.

tips.title: Switch to Sequence for long chains over large collections
tips.content:
Collection operators like map/filter on a List are eager — each call
allocates a fully new intermediate list, so a chain of five operators over
100k items allocates five 100k-element lists.

asSequence() makes the same chain lazy: each element flows through all
operators one at a time, with no intermediate collections. For short chains
or small collections, eager operations are actually faster due to sequence
overhead — reserve asSequence() for long operator chains over large data.

tips.title: associateBy builds a lookup map in one pass
tips.content:
A common mistake is calling filter { it.id == targetId }.firstOrNull()
repeatedly inside a loop, which is O(n) per lookup and O(n*m) overall.

associateBy converts a list into a Map keyed by a selector in a single pass,
turning repeated lookups into O(1) map access — build the map once outside
the loop, not inside it.

tips.title: groupBy plus eachCount replaces manual tally loops
tips.content:
Counting occurrences by category with a mutable HashMap and manual
increment logic is verbose and easy to get wrong (forgetting to initialize
a missing key, for example).

groupingBy { }.eachCount() does this in one line, handling the missing-key
case automatically and returning a Map<K, Int> directly.

tips.title: Distinguish List (read-only view) from MutableList (mutable)
tips.content:
Kotlin's List interface has no add/remove methods, but that doesn't
guarantee immutability — it's a read-only view that can still be backed by
a mutable list elsewhere, and mutations through that other reference are
visible through your List reference too.

For true immutability guarantees (e.g. thread-safety, defensive copies at
an API boundary), use toList() to snapshot a copy, or a genuinely immutable
collection library like kotlinx.collections.immutable.
tips.codeSnippet:
val mutable = mutableListOf(1, 2, 3)
val readOnlyView: List<Int> = mutable // just a view, not a copy
mutable.add(4)
println(readOnlyView) // [1, 2, 3, 4] — changed! same backing list

val snapshot = mutable.toList() // true independent copy

tips.title: partition splits a collection into two lists in one pass
tips.content:
Filtering the same list twice with opposite predicates (filter { pred } and
filter { !pred }) iterates the collection twice for what is logically one
classification pass.

partition returns a Pair of lists — matching and non-matching — computed in
a single traversal, which is both more efficient and reads more clearly at
the call site.
tips.codeSnippet:
val (completed, pending) = tasks.partition { it.isDone }

// vs: val completed = tasks.filter { it.isDone }; val pending = tasks.filter { !it.isDone }

tips.title: fold accumulates state that reduce can't express
tips.content:
reduce uses the collection's first element as the initial accumulator and
fails on an empty collection. fold takes an explicit initial value, so it
handles empty collections gracefully and lets the accumulator be a
different type than the elements.

Use fold whenever you're building up a different-typed result (a map, a
string, a custom object) from a list, rather than reducing to the same
element type.
tips.codeSnippet:
val summary: Map<String, Int> = orders.fold(mutableMapOf()) { acc, order ->
    acc.merge(order.category, order.quantity, Int::plus)
    acc
}

val total = emptyList<Int>().fold(0) { acc, n -> acc + n } // 0, no crash

tips.title: map and filter — the essentials
tips.content:
'map' transforms each element in a collection, producing a new list.
'filter' keeps only elements matching a predicate.

These are the two most common collection operations. 
They don't modify the original list — they create new ones (immutable by default).

Chain them together for powerful data transformations in just a few lines.

tips.title: groupBy — organize data instantly
tips.content:
'groupBy' splits a collection into a Map<Key, List<Value>> 
based on a key selector function.

Incredibly useful for categorizing data: 
group users by role, orders by status, logs by date, etc.

Combine with mapValues to transform the grouped lists further.

tips.title: Sequence for large collections
tips.content:
Regular collection operations (map, filter) create intermediate lists at each step.
For large collections, this wastes memory.

Sequences process elements lazily — one at a time, through all operations, 
without creating intermediate collections.

Use .asSequence() when chaining multiple operations on large lists. 
For small collections (< 100 elements), regular lists are faster due to less overhead.
